clue.text: Transfer over a million pounds at first for 17/6

indicators.note: one word is laid over the other on both sides, so the money transfer wraps round the sum

parts.note: to vire is to move funds from one budget heading to another, as in virement

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the word pounds is wanted, its head standing in for it

parts.note: taken as written
M is the abbreviation for million
the first letter of pounds

explanation.surface: A dodgy money transfer of over a million pounds, the kind a bloodsucking financier might arrange.
explanation.walkthrough: VIRE (an accountant's word) goes round A, M and P to make VAMPIRE. 17/6 means 17-across and 6-down read together: BLOOD SUCKER, the puzzle's theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Vampires feed on human blood, so they are the classic bloodsuckers of folklore and horror fiction.

clue.text: Greed of girl going both ways with 1 author

indicators.note: a name that goes both ways reads the same forwards and backwards

parts.note: a girl's name that reads the same in either direction
Anne Rice wrote Interview with the Vampire, so she is the author of 1-across fiction

explanation.surface: A greedy girl and a vampire novelist, as if describing a writer's mercenary companion.
explanation.walkthrough: '1 author' refers back to the answer to 1-across: Anne Rice is the best-known modern writer of vampire novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Avarice is an extreme desire for wealth, one of the seven deadly sins, and so a synonym of greed.

clue.text: Dad consuming endless wine and food

indicators.note: with no end, the wine loses its final letter
Dad swallowing something means it ends up inside him

parts.note: an informal word for father
Asti, the Italian sparkling wine, without its last letter

explanation.surface: Father getting through the wine and the dinner, a picture of a hearty family meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Pasta is a staple Italian dish of dough shapes such as spaghetti, so it is a kind of food.

clue.text: Traveller collecting a stamp in country

indicators.note: the traveller picks up one more item, adding it to the end of the group

parts.note: the Romani people are traditionally itinerant, and in Britain Travellers is a name for such communities
the single item collected, a stamp being one thing to add to a collection

explanation.surface: A tourist picking up a souvenir stamp in a foreign land, like a passport stamp at the border.
explanation.walkthrough: The traveller collects 'a': A is added to the end of ROMANI. The stamp is mostly surface dressing, the thing a traveller collects.
explanation.definitionFit: Romania is a nation in south-eastern Europe, with Bucharest as its capital, so it is a country.

clue.text: Last lines of sonnet recalled trapping end of penis in flies

indicators.note: called back, so the poem's closing section is read from its end
trapping something means holding it inside
only the last letter of the following word is wanted

parts.note: the final six lines of a Petrarchan sonnet form the sestet
the last letter of penis

explanation.surface: A bawdy poem whose closing lines catch something rude in a zip, a schoolboy picture.
explanation.walkthrough: TETSES takes S after its first letter. Tsetse flies of Africa are bloodsuckers, fitting the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Tsetses are African biting flies that spread sleeping sickness, so the plural noun matches flies.

clue.text: Shoot gull

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a new growth springing from a plant's root or stem
second meaning: a dupe, someone easily fooled

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like an order to fire at a seabird; both words are nouns with other senses. With 17-across it also completes the theme word BLOOD SUCKER.
explanation.definitionFit: Gardeners call a stray shoot from a rootstock by this name, and a gullible victim is also called one.

clue.text: Deeper level supporting cast in audition

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting part sits underneath, so it comes second
an audition is a hearing, so the word is taken by how it sounds

parts.note: one who casts is a thrower, which in a non-rhotic accent ends in an unstressed 'uh' sound
a tier is one level of a structure

explanation.surface: An actor at an audition being placed in the supporting cast at a lower level.
explanation.walkthrough: One who casts is a thrower, and in a British accent that word ends in an unstressed 'uh', so the sound is spelt THROA. The homophone is loose.
explanation.definitionFit: A throatier voice is lower and more guttural, so it sounds deeper; both are comparative adjectives.

clue.text: Female leaving attractive impression

indicators.note: the female abbreviation goes away from the word that follows

parts.note: fetching means charming or good-looking
F is the abbreviation for female

explanation.surface: A woman walking out of a room and leaving a strong impression on everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaving attractive impression' reads as a phrase about charm, but it is F removed from FETCHING.
explanation.definitionFit: An etching is a print taken from an etched plate, and a print or copy can be called an impression.

clue.text: Retired people bending over backwards perhaps to expel Tory 17/6s

parts.note: former, no longer active

indicators.note: expelling the Tory means throwing that word out of the phrase

parts.note: performers who bend their bodies into extreme shapes, such as backbends
Con is the short form of Conservative

explanation.surface: Former circus performers doing backbends to oust a Conservative politician.
explanation.walkthrough: EX-CONTORTIONISTS loses CON. A Tory is a member of Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: Extortionists bleed their victims of money, so figuratively they are bloodsuckers living off others.

clue.text: Bonkers attempt to make a comeback

indicators.note: coming back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the word is read from its end

parts.note: to have a stab is to have a try

explanation.surface: Calling a sporting comeback attempt crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Bats is British slang for mad, as in having bats in the belfry, matching the informal bonkers.

clue.text: Marx brothers finally check out star of 19

indicators.note: out here means wrong or disordered, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: only the closing letter of brothers is wanted

parts.note: the last letter of brothers
taken as written

explanation.surface: A suggestion to check out the Marx Brothers films, as if recommending classic comedians.
explanation.walkthrough: 19 is NOSFERATU, the 1922 silent film; its vampire Count Orlok was played by the German actor of this name.
explanation.definitionFit: This German actor played Count Orlok in Murnau's silent film, so he is that movie's leading performer.

clue.text: Bird mum keeps at home

indicators.note: mum keeping something holds it within her

parts.note: an informal word for mother
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: Mother keeping a pet bird in the house.
explanation.definitionFit: Mina is a variant spelling of mynah, an Asian starling known for mimicking human speech.

clue.text: Are Converse stocked by dispenser of style at Covent Garden?

indicators.note: something stocked by a dispenser is held inside it

parts.note: an optic is a measuring device fixed to an upturned spirit bottle in a bar

indicators.note: the converse is the opposite way round, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Asking whether a shop dispensing fashion in Covent Garden sells Converse trainers.
explanation.walkthrough: Converse looks like the trainer brand. An optic is a British bar fitting that pours exact measures. Covent Garden is home to the Royal Opera House.
explanation.definitionFit: The Royal Opera House stands in Covent Garden, so the style there is that of grand opera.

clue.text: English footballers entertained by Rolling Stone's version of Don't Stop Believin'

indicators.note: guests entertained by a host are taken in, so they sit inside

parts.note: Keith Richards, guitarist of the Rolling Stones
E is the abbreviation for English
the Professional Footballers' Association, the players' union in England

explanation.surface: A rock star recording a cover of the Journey anthem, with England players along for the ride.
explanation.walkthrough: Don't Stop Believin' is the Journey song; the definition is a rewording of its title.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep faith is to go on trusting or believing, so it restates the song's plea not to stop believing.

clue.text: Stuck out reminder about pastry's filling

indicators.note: going about something means surrounding it

parts.note: a prod is a nudge to jog someone's memory

indicators.note: the filling of the pastry is its inside, without the outer letters

parts.note: the inner letters of strudel, the pastry the clue means

explanation.surface: A note sticking out of a pastry, perhaps a slip about what fills it.
explanation.walkthrough: The pastry is strudel, the Austrian layered pastry; its filling drops the S and L.
explanation.definitionFit: Protruded means jutted out beyond a surface, a past-tense verb just like stuck out.

clue.text: Digger regularly on motorway is a nuisance in Scotland

indicators.note: in an across clue, one part placed on another follows it

parts.note: the M1, the main motorway north out of London, written as MI

indicators.note: taking letters at regular intervals means every other one

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters of digger

explanation.surface: A mechanical digger working on a motorway, causing roadworks misery.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is England's London-to-Leeds motorway, with 1 read as I. The Highland midge swarms in Scottish summers and bites.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish midge is a tiny biting fly infamous for plaguing walkers in the Highlands, a famous pest there.

clue.text: Kids swapping sides to make descent

indicators.note: the sides are right and left, so one of those letters is exchanged for the other

parts.note: a brood is a family of young children

explanation.surface: Children switching teams in the playground and making an exit.
explanation.walkthrough: In BROOD the R (right) is swapped for L (left).
explanation.definitionFit: Blood means lineage or ancestry, as in of noble blood, so it matches descent in the family sense.

clue.text: Sea creature picked up young victim

indicators.note: picked up here means caught by the ear, as a radio picks up a signal

parts.note: a lamb is a young sheep and prey is a hunted victim

explanation.surface: A predator in the sea snatching a young victim.
explanation.walkthrough: Lamb prey said aloud gives the fish; the silent B drops out of the spelling. The lamprey sucks blood, keeping the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: The lamprey is a jawless eel-like fish found in seas and rivers that latches on to other fish.

clue.text: 17/6 for Austen novel

indicators.note: novel means new and different, so the letters take a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Looking for a bloodsucker in a Jane Austen novel, as in a horror-Austen mash-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Austen novel' reads as a book title, but novel is the anagram signal. 17/6 is BLOOD SUCKER.
explanation.definitionFit: Nosferatu is a name for a vampire, from Murnau's 1922 film, so it fits the bloodsucker theme.

clue.text: Doctor can feel Banquo's issue

indicators.note: to doctor is to tamper with, so these letters are altered in order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A physician sensing what is wrong with a patient called Banquo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like a physician, but it is the anagram signal. In Macbeth the witches prophesy that Banquo's descendants will be kings.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's Macbeth, Banquo's son escapes the murderers, and issue means offspring or children.

clue.text: Heart is broken by Brockwell's latest puzzle

indicators.note: breaking into something means getting inside it

parts.note: ticker is slang for the heart

indicators.note: the latest part of the setter's name is its last letter

parts.note: the last letter of the setter's pseudonym

explanation.surface: A heartbreaking crossword from the setter himself, a sly boast about this very puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: Brockwell is this puzzle's setter, so the self-reference is a deliberate wink.
explanation.definitionFit: A tickler is a tricky problem, as in brain-tickler, so it can stand for a puzzle.

clue.text: Attributes of Gaia, the nature goddess

indicators.note: attributes of a phrase are things it contains, so the letters lie within it

parts.note: found across the end of Gaia, all of the and the start of nature

explanation.surface: Describing the qualities of Gaia, the Greek earth goddess.
explanation.walkthrough: Gaia looks like the goddess wanted, but she is only the cover for the hidden one.
explanation.definitionFit: Athena is the Greek deity of wisdom and warfare, patron of Athens.

clue.text: Hack maybe with Times tucking into top-notch biscuits

indicators.note: tucking into means going inside

parts.note: A1 means first-rate, written with the 1 as I
a hack is a riding horse, of which a mare is one kind
T is short for time, so two of them

explanation.surface: A journalist from The Times tucking into posh biscuits at a press lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: Hack looks like a journalist, especially next to Times, but it is a horse here.
explanation.definitionFit: Amaretti are small Italian almond-flavoured macaroons, a type of biscuit.

clue.text: Walker is one with no answer for parasites

indicators.note: having none of something means it has been removed

parts.note: Alice Walker, American author of The Color Purple
A is the abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: A hiker who has no answer to bloodsucking pests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Walker' looks like a hiker; it is the novelist Alice Walker.
explanation.definitionFit: Lice are small wingless insects that live on hosts and feed on their blood, the plural of louse.

clue.text: Old doctor from General Hospital snorting cocaine

indicators.note: snorting a drug takes it in, so it goes inside

parts.note: Robert E. Lee, Confederate general in the American Civil War
C is slang shorthand for cocaine
H is the map abbreviation for hospital

explanation.surface: A disgraced old doctor from a general hospital caught taking cocaine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'General Hospital' reads as a single place, but it splits into LEE and H.
explanation.definitionFit: Leech is an archaic word for a physician, who once bled patients with leeches.

clue.text: Republican heavyweight following game show on Netflix

indicators.note: the politician and weight come after the card game

parts.note: the card game
R is the abbreviation for Republican
a ton is a heavy weight

explanation.surface: A Republican political heavyweight who once hosted a game show, now in a Netflix series.
explanation.definitionFit: Bridgerton is a period drama series on Netflix, based on Julia Quinn's Regency romance novels.

clue.text: Slice from return of Kyle Edmund is like 18

indicators.note: returning goes back the other way, so the letters are read in reverse
a slice is a piece cut out of the words that follow

parts.note: the end of Kyle and start of Edmund

explanation.surface: A tennis player, Kyle Edmund, slicing a return of serve.
explanation.walkthrough: Kyle Edmund is a British tennis player, so slice and return pose as tennis shots. 18 is LAMPREY.
explanation.definitionFit: A lamprey is a long slender jawless fish shaped like an eel, so it is eely.

clue.text: Writer of Lady In Red ultimately inspired by pop duo

indicators.note: inspired here is breathed in, so these letters go inside

parts.note: Wham! were George Michael and Andrew Ridgeley

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so each word gives its final letter

parts.note: the last letters of lady, in and red

explanation.surface: Asking who wrote the Chris de Burgh hit and whether an eighties pop duo inspired it.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lady in Red was a Chris de Burgh hit; Wham! were the 1980s British pop duo.
explanation.definitionFit: John Wyndham was the English novelist who wrote The Day of the Triffids, so he is a writer.

clue.text: Noel Gallagher on vacation abroad eating hot chicken

indicators.note: eating something takes it inside
abroad suggests wandering far off, so the letters move around

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: vacated means emptied, so the inside of the surname is cleared out

parts.note: the first and last letters of Gallagher
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: Noel Gallagher of Oasis on holiday overseas, eating spicy chicken.
explanation.walkthrough: Noel Gallagher, of the band Oasis, is whole; only his surname is emptied. Leghorn is also the old English name for Livorno, apt with abroad.
